analytic.title: Finding a steady state point for fixed priority independent periodic real-time tasks with arbitrary given release offsets

div.p: Minimal schedulability interval is one of the important considerations of both research motivation and practice stage. In this paper, we investigate the problem of finding a starting time point of the minimal schedulability interval for fixed priority independent periodic real-time preemptive tasks with arbitrary given release offsets (phasing). A linked list-based method is proposed for solving the problem. Each node in the linked list represents a pending-less busy period. Analysis and experimental results show that the linked list-based method outperforms the current best acyclic-idle-slot-based one.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: In real-time systems, a set of tasks can be synchronous, i.e., all tasks arrive at the same time such as at the time point 0, or asynchronous, i.e., all of tasks never share a common release time though some of them may do so [7], [8]. For asynchronous tasks, they must be initially released asynchronously with some offsets (or phasing). To date, there have been different preemptive real-time system models, such as the classic preemptive model [17] (shortened as the classic model) and the Priority-based Functional Reactive Programming (P-FRP) model [20], [22], and there have been different scheduling policies, such as the Rate Monotonic (RM), the Deadline Monotonic (DM), the Earliest Deadline First (EDF), and the Least Laxity First (LLF) [15], [16], [17], [19].

For description concision and convenience we use the Burns Standard Notation [9], such as the number of tasks n, for 1 ≤ i ≤ n, the priority P i (1 is the highest priority index), the worst-case execution time C i , the relative deadline D i , the period T i , the hyperperiod H, and the utilization U i , for a task τ i . In addition, we use Φ i , relative to the time point 0, to denote the initial or transformed release offset (or phasing) of a task τ i , r to denote the maximum value of all task offsets, i.e., r = max sum of the offset and period, i.e., maxrT
div.formula: = max n i=1 {Φ i +T i }. Let maxT = max n i=1 {T i }. A (general) level-i busy period is a time interval [a, b
div.p: ] within which jobs of priority i or higher are processed throughout [a, b] but no jobs of level i or higher are processed in (a-, a) or (b, b + ) for sufficiently small > 0 [14]. We give another definition in this paper. A pending-less level-i busy period is a time interval [a, b) within which jobs of priority i or higher are processed throughout [a, b) and there is no lower priority pending job in [a, b). A pending job is a job that is released and does not complete its execution. Note that a pending-less busy period may or may not be a general busy period.

In the classic model, it is known that the RM scheduler is optimal for fixed priority periodic synchronous independent tasks with implicit deadlines (i.e., the deadline is equal to the period for each task) on one processor. The schedulability interval is therefore be [0, maxT ), with a starting time point 0 [17]. RM means that a task with smaller period will be assigned a higher priority. However, for asynchronous tasks the schedulability problem is co-NP-hard in the strong sense [15], [16], [4], [3], and thus it is of significance to reduce a schedulability (or feasibility) interval length in practice though at present this length in theory is related to the hyperperiod (i.e., the least common multiple of all task periods), which is not a polynomial function of the number of tasks.

In this paper, we consider a discrete fixed priority hard realtime system on one processor with independent periodic tasks which are constrained deadlines (i.e., D i ≤ T i ), with arbitrary given release offsets, and scheduled by work-conserving policy. We investigate the problem of finding a steady state point in order to minimize the simulation interval of exact schedulability test for such preemptive tasks. The system starts at time 0, i.e., min n i=1 {Φ i } = 0. A steady state (time) point s means that for any time point t ≥ s the schedule at the time point t + H is the same as that at the time point t. It is known that a schedule with periodicity can be represented by using the star operator as the repetition of its preceding interval, and [a, b)[b, c) * represents the schedule over the interval [a, b) followed by the schedule over [b, c) repeated cyclically [11], where b is a steady state point. In this way, respectively efficient methods can be used in the step of finding a steady state point and the step of following exact schedulability test.

Different researchers have studied the simulation interval of exact schedulability test in many ways in the literature. In [15] Leung et al. proved a schedulability interval to be [0, r+2 * H), where the steady state point used was r + H. In [1] Audsley introduced an approach for transforming offsets to calculate the initial stabilization time, S i , as a steady state point for the first i higher priority tasks, and the schedulability interval was then [0, S n + H) for an n-task set. In [10] Goossens et al. provided another method to inductively calculate S i as a steady state point for the first i higher priority tasks and then the schedulability interval was [0, S n + H). Note that these two upper bound steady state points S n s might be different due to different calculating approaches. In [13] we introduced a transformation step before simulating a schedule to make each arbitrary release offset Φ i shorter than the task period
div.formula: T i . The transformation for Φ i is: if (Φ i ≥ T i ) then Φ i ← Φ i -Φ i /T i * T i .
div.p: Then the method in [10] was employed. The main limitation of these methods, however, was that though the calculation was in a linear time the calculated steady state point S n could be very large and thus the schedulability test has to be conducted over a very long interval [0, S n +H) (that could be several hyperperiods long for some task periods and release scenarios [11]), even after the transformation step.

Based on their insights into the schedule periodicity and the processor idleness, Choqiet-Geniet et al. [6] proved a minimal schedulability interval to be [θ c , θ c + H) where θ c ≥ 0 and θ c -1 denotes the time point of the last acyclic idle slot, and the simulation interval for the following schedulability test will be [0, θ c + H) [11]. However, for deriving θ c , each time slot in a test interval [0, r + H) with a length r + H should be checked to determine the time of the last acyclic idle slot. This means that in general an interval length (r + H) + (θ c + H), which is no less than the length as in [15], has to be dealt with for the whole process of a simulation schedulability test.

Our solution for finding a steady state point is that we use a linked list for representing the schedule in the finding process. We have employed a linked list for testing the schedulability of fixed priority independent periodic tasks in both the classic model [18] and the P-FRP model [12]. For convenience, we also referred to our method as the LList-based method, though we solve a very different problem in this paper.

Our experiments show that the run time performance of the LList-based method outperforms the current best acyclic-idleslot-based algorithm [6], especially in the scenario where the hyperperiod H is greater than maxT , since the search length for finding a steady state point in the LList-based method is only maxrT = max n i=1 {Φ i +T i } instead of r +H in [6]. The LList-based method also performs better than the current best acyclic-idle-slot-based algorithm even for tasks with harmonic periods where H = maxT .

div.head: II. OUR METHOD
div.p: We note that for independent periodic tasks with offsets, after time point maxrT the schedule in time interval [maxrT, maxrT + H) repeats itself infinitely and the first steady state time point is no later than the time point maxrT . Thus, we will find a steady state point by simulating its schedule within a time interval [0, maxrT ]. Note that though the time point maxrT is a starting point of the repeated segment with a hyperperiod length, however, there may be carry-in jobs [2] after that time point and thus the time point maxrT cannot in general be taken as a starting point for the following schedulability test.

For arbitrary given release offsets, when a task's (initial) release offset is much greater than its period, the maximum offset r of all tasks would be very large. In this paper, first we use the above transformation step for each offset Φ i , and then calculate maxrT = max n i=1 {Φ i + T i } where Φ i is the transformed offset and simulate the schedule of the finding process in the time interval [0, maxrT ].

Similar to our previous studies [12], [18], in this paper the schedule of a task set is also represented by a linked list and a linked list node represents a pending-less busy period in the schedule. Each list node has three fields: the beginning time of the busy period, the end time of the busy period, and the pointer to the next node. The simulation is performed task per task in the priority order, from the highest priority task to the lowest one. Two nodes representing two adjoining pendingless busy periods are usually merged into one node to represent a longer busy period.

Different from our previous studies using linked list in exact schedulability test [12], [18], a key step for finding a proper steady state point in the paper is that, when scheduling a job of task τ j , if the job of τ j starts at the end of or completes at the beginning of a pending-less level-i busy period (i < j), then the current level-i and level-j pending-less busy periods will not be merged; otherwise, two adjoining pending-less busy period will be merged into one longer pending-less busy period. In this way, it guarantees that there is no carry-in job just after the steady state time point found in the method and thus the following exact schedulability test can start from this steady state time point instead of from time 0.

In our method, one key factor for performance improvement is simulating a pending-less busy period by one linked list node instead of simulating it in a time-tick way as the acyclicidle-slot-based algorithm does. When simulation completes, the beginning time of the last busy period is the steady state point. Another key factor for performance improvement is that the search length for finding a steady state point is shortened from r + H in [6] to maxrT = max n i=1 {Φ i + T i }. In our method, when a steady state point s is found, the simulation interval for the following schedulability test can then be conducted within the time interval [s, s + H) (with an exact length H) instead of [0, s + H). The steady state point found by our method is not necessarily the first one in the schedule as that found in [6]. However, this does not affect the performance of the following schedulability test since the schedulability interval length is exact H.

As in our previous studies [12], [18], we also use a memory array for improving the efficiency of the LList-based method. A memory array is allocated as a whole before the simulation and then the following operations of memory allocation and recycling for each node are performed in the user space instead Locating the release time of the job τi,j in the Sched list from the current position pointed by the P ointer; 12:

It is about three times improvement in average. The comparison table is omitted due to space limitation.

For an n-task set, the total number of jobs, N , in the time interval [0, maxrT ] is N = n i=1 (maxrT -Φ i )/T i + n and only these jobs are simulated in the LList-based method. This number is sensitive to the span and the distribution of task periods. Since one pending-less busy period in the schedule is represented by merely one node and the simulation is performed task per task in the task priority order, the total running time is mainly determined by the time of operating the linked list nodes, and thus the time complexity of the LList-based method is related to the number of nodes used in the simulation. Particularly, as long as task periods span only one order of magnitude, only O(n) time is needed for simulating an n-task set, regardless of the length of the maximum period of the task set as well as the total utilization. In the above mentioned case, the total number of list nodes used in simulation is very small, and this is the root cause why the LList-based method performs better [18].

The skeleton of the LList-based method for finding a steady state point with no carry-in job is described in Algorithm 1. The time complexity of the LList-based method is in polynomial-time O(N ) where N is the total number of jobs within the time interval [0, maxrT ], and the total number of nodes used in the linked list is no more than N in the worst case. However, the acyclic-idle-slot-based method is exponential with respect to the maximum phasing and the hyperperiod since its search length is r + H.

div.head: III. EXPERIMENT AND PRELIMINARY RESULTS
div.p: On the one hand, we generate 7 groups of randomly sampled periodic task sets, with 3 to 9 tasks, by varying tasks' parameters and task set size. An n-task set is generated as follows: Use the UUniFast algorithm [5] to generate n utilization factors U i in a decreasing order, 1 ≤ i ≤ n, such that the total utilization U = n i=1 U i equal to a given value in [0.6, 0.9]; Task periods were then uniformly and randomly generated from a given range [5,40], sort them in an increasing order, and set them in sequence to the period T i , 1 ≤ i ≤ n; And then let the computation time C i = U i * T i . Each initial release offset Φ i is uniformly and randomly generated such that 0 ≤ Φ i < T i . On the other hand, we also generate 7 groups of harmonic period task sets, from 4-task to 256-task sets in the similar way except that the harmonic period range is [16,1024] and the offset Φ i is such that 0 ≤ Φ i < 8 * T i for simulating the scenario that r = max n i=1 {Φ i } is greater than some T i . RM scheduling is employed. Each of the task sets in each group is likely to be unique since they are generated independently. There are 1 000 task sets in each group. The experiment is conducted on a PC with CPU i7-4770 3.4GHz and 16GB memory.

Fig. 1 shows how the average running time required by the acyclic-idle-slot-based algorithm [6] and by our LListbased method varied with the number of randomly generated tasks per taskset. In this secnario, the hyperperiod increases likely with the increasing number of tasks. From the figure we can see that the average running time of the LList-based method goes nearly steady while the acyclic-idle-slot-based algorithm increases exponentially with the increasing number of tasks per taskset. The performance of the LList-based method outperforms the acyclic-idle-slot-based one. Note that for these tasksets the task period range [5,40] spans only one order of magnitude; however, for the 9-task sets the maximum hyperperiod has been greater than 1.7 billion which makes the running time of the acyclic-idle-slot-based algorithm very long. Due to very large hyperperiod and unacceptable running time of the acyclic-idle-slot-based method, we do not provide performance comparisons between the LList-based and the acyclic-idle-slot-based methods for scenarios where the task periods span multiple orders of magnitude, while the performance of the LList-based method in these scenarios can be seen in [18].

In addition, Fig. 2 shows a performance comparison between the LList-based and the acyclic-idle-slot-based methods for scenarios of harmonic task periods. From the figure we can see that in these harmonic period scenarios, though the difference of search lengths for the two methods is not very large (since the hyperperiod is equal to the maximum period), the LList-based method also performs better than the acyclicidle-slot-based algorithm, with nearly a half average running time per taskset in each group.

Table II shows the maximum number of list nodes used in the LList-based method versus the number of tasks in the scenarios of harmonic periods (the maximum number of list nodes used in scenarios in Fig. 1 is only 71). From the table, we can see that the maximum memory space needed by the linked list is not more than 10KB and thus is completely affordable.

It should be stated that though the experimental results shown in the paper are derived in the classic model, the LListbased method can also be used in the P-FRP model and some of its variants for solving the problem of finding a steady state point, as for addressing the problems of the schedulability test and response time analysis in our previous work [12], [21].

div.head: IV. CONCLUSION
div.p: The work presented in this paper focuses on finding a steady state point in order to minimize the simulation interval of schedulability test and is part of our ongoing research on the schedulability test and response time analysis for fixed priority periodic real-time tasks with arbitrary release offsets. Experimental results have shown that the LList-based method is a better candidate in these studies. More comprehensive experiments will be conducted to investigate the suitable scope of the LList-based method. Furthermore, extending the LListbased method to simulate dynamic priority scheduling such as EDF scheduling is also one of our future work.
